subject: math
title: JC H2 functions and graphs: transformations, reciprocal functions, asymptote behaviour

slides.heading: JC H2 functions and graphs: transformations, reciprocal functions, asymptote behaviour
bullets: How transformations move and stretch a graph, and how reciprocal functions are ruled by their asymptotes
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we start from one graph, y = f(x), and learn to predict exactly what every change to its equation does to its shape, ending with reciprocal functions and their asymptotes.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Describe stretches and translations of y = f(x), including changes inside the brackets
Sketch reciprocal functions from their asymptotes - while remembering that inside the brackets means shift LEFT
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the plus-inside trap.

slides.heading: Same graph, new equation
bullets: The graph of y = f(x + 3) looks like the original graph - but moved
Does the plus sign push it to the right, the way plus usually means more?
slides.notes: Ask the class: plus usually means more, so which way should f(x + 3) move? Take two or three answers, then say: hold that thought, because the honest answer surprises almost everyone the first time.

slides.heading: Outside moves vertically, inside moves horizontally
bullets: Changes outside f act vertically: a·f(x) stretches heights by a factor of a, and + d lifts the graph by d
Changes inside f act horizontally and feel backwards: f(bx + c) is read as f(b(x + c/b))
A reciprocal function such as y = 1/x is ruled by its asymptotes: lines the curve approaches but never touches
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: outside is vertical and honest, inside is horizontal and backwards - every question in this topic is one of those two moves.

slides.heading: y = a·f(x) + d: stretch the height, then lift the graph
bullets: Multiplying by a stretches every y-coordinate: y = 2f(x) is twice as tall as y = f(x)
Adding d at the end lifts the whole stretched graph up by d
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch every height double first, then watch the whole curve lift - stretch first, then shift, exactly as the equation reads left to right.

slides.heading: y = f(bx + c): read it as f(b(x + c/b))
bullets: Factor out b first: f(2x + 2) is f(2(x + 1)), so the squeeze is centred after a shift left of 1
The factor b squeezes the graph horizontally toward that centre by a factor of b
slides.notes: Tell them to watch the graph shift left first, then squeeze toward its new centre: factoring out b is the move that makes the true centre visible instead of guessed.

slides.heading: Reciprocal functions: the asymptotes run the show
bullets: y = 1/x has a vertical asymptote x = 0 and a horizontal asymptote y = 0
As x grows the curve flattens onto y = 0; as x approaches 0 the curve shoots up x = 0, and the sign flips across it
slides.notes: Watch the two branches hug their asymptotes: the curve can approach an asymptote forever, flatten onto the horizontal one, but it never crosses the vertical one.

slides.heading: The +c trap: inside the brackets means shift LEFT
bullets: f(x + 3) is zero where x = -3, so every point of the graph sits 3 units further left
Plus inside the brackets shifts LEFT; minus inside the brackets shifts RIGHT
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: the animation first shows the wrong rightward shift, crosses it out, and then slides the graph left to where the root check says it must be.

slides.heading: Worked example: describe y = 2f(x) + 1
bullets: Step 1: the factor 2 outside f stretches every height of y = f(x) by a factor of 2
Step 2: the + 1 outside f lifts the stretched graph up by 1 - a vertical stretch, then a translation up
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: both changes are outside f, so both act vertically and both read in the honest direction.

slides.heading: Your turn: transform, then correct
bullets: Describe the transformation that maps y = f(x) onto y = f(2x + 2), factoring out the 2 first
Careful - a classmate writes: f(x + 3) shifts the graph 3 units to the right. Explain to them why that is wrong, using the root check
slides.notes: Give pairs two minutes, then cold-call one pair and press them on the trap: if f(x + 3) is zero where x = -3, which way did the graph really move?

slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
bullets: Describe a stretch and a translation, and sketch a reciprocal function from its asymptotes
Explain why this claim is wrong: f(x + 3) shifts the graph 3 units to the right.
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the root check in your last answer - if you can show f(x + 3) is zero at x = -3, you have cracked today's lesson.
